Keep those secrets out of messages, support forms and this learning website.

There are also shared-control, hardware-assisted and other wallet designs. Some use multiple approvals; others provide different recovery arrangements. A recovery phrase is not a universal feature of every wallet. The useful question is about the specific model rather than a slogan about ownership.

Consider a fictional comparison. Service A offers password recovery but publishes its own withdrawal conditions. Wallet B lets its user authorise transfers directly and provides a documented recovery process. That does not make A automatically safe or B automatically suitable. The responsibilities differ. Read current instructions and consider whether you can maintain the required recovery arrangement.

An address may be shared for receiving where appropriate. A private key or recovery phrase is a different kind of information. A person asking for those secrets is not merely asking where to send money. A signature request also needs inspection: some authorise consequential actions, rather than simply confirming a sign-in.

Before you rely on a wallet, be able to explain its control, recovery and support arrangements in ordinary words. Check instructions through an independently reached official source. If important details remain unclear, pause. This article asks you to understand the model; it does not ask you to create a wallet, disclose a secret or transfer funds.

articles.title: What proves a crypto payment reached its destination?
articles.body_html:
A message saying “sent” can describe the start of a process. It does not establish every later result. A screenshot, a network transaction, a service's credited balance and a local-money payout answer different questions.

What does the sender claim? A screenshot can show an amount, an address and a convincing tick. It can also be edited, incomplete or taken from another transaction. Treat it as a claim to verify. A transaction identifier gives you something to investigate; it is not proof by itself.

What does the correct network record show? Establish the network first, then inspect a trustworthy route to that record. Check the actual status, destination, relevant asset or token movement and amount. Pending means the outcome is still unresolved. Included does not always mean the intended action succeeded: a failed smart-contract execution can still appear on a network and may incur a fee. Interpret the relevant record rather than a colour alone.

Has the receiving service credited it? A service may require the supported asset/network combination, destination details, a minimum deposit and a stated confirmation or processing condition. Those are specific instructions, not one universal rule. A successful transfer to a service-controlled address does not independently prove that your account has been credited.

Has the promised payout arrived? A credited crypto balance is different from a completed conversion and from money arriving in a bank or mobile-money account. Check the relevant provider and destination records for each step. Network finality cannot confirm a separate bank transfer.

Here is a fictional example. A receiving service says it requires five confirmations followed by processing. The supplied network record shows five confirmations and the service independently shows Credited. That supports the crypto-credit result under these supplied conditions. If a later local payout still says Pending, local-money receipt remains unconfirmed. We can recognise the established result without pretending the whole chain is finished.

Do not rely on an apparent payment to release goods until the evidence meets the relevant receiving conditions. If something does not match, use independently reached official support and keep the uncertainty explicit. A stranger's link or “release fee” demand does not become trustworthy because it arrived with a screenshot.

articles.title: Same coin name, different route
articles.body_html:
Imagine the sender's screen says USDC and the receiver's screen also says USDC. It looks like a match. Before sending, there is another question: are both sides describing the same supported asset on the same network?

A ticker is a short label. It is not a complete asset identity. A token can have deployments on different networks, and another representation can use a familiar label. A provider decides which exact combinations it accepts through a particular receiving route. Matching names cannot answer that question for you.

Check three things together.

The asset or representation: Is this the issuer-native deployment the receiver accepts, or something wrapped or otherwise different? Do not infer equivalence from a logo, ticker or displayed price. Use the exact identifying information supplied in current official instructions.

The selected network: Which network will carry the transfer? A familiar address format may appear across networks. An address that passes a format check does not establish that the receiving service credits transfers through the selected network.

The receiving conditions: Does the receiver explicitly support this asset on that network through this destination? Check required memo/tag details, minimums and relevant deposit conditions. “We support USDC” can be less specific than the instructions you need.

For a fictional practice example, Service A offers issuer-native USDC on Ethereum. Service B's current supplied instructions accept issuer-native USDC through Base only. The common token name does not establish a compatible route. Pause and find an explicitly supported combination. This invented setup does not claim that any real provider currently has those exact services.

Even a compatible combination is only one part of transfer review. The intended recipient, complete destination, amount, fees and meaningful conditions still need checking. You may also decide to use another payment method. A low fee cannot repair a route mismatch.

Address look familiar? Still check the route.

If something has already been sent incorrectly, recovery depends on the exact asset, network, receiving authority and provider policy. Some cases may be unrecoverable. Do not promise recovery or make a second payment to someone claiming they can fix it. Reach the genuine receiving service through an independently verified channel.

articles.title: The screenshot that needed one more question
articles.body_html:
This story is invented for learning. The people, service names, transaction records and conditions are fictional. It describes no reported incident, actual provider or country-specific payment instruction.

Nia sells a second-hand desk. A prospective buyer, Kojo, asks whether she can receive a crypto payment through a service called Harbour. Their fictional agreement requires the corresponding local-money payout to be independently recorded before she releases the desk. She has read the receiving instructions in the supplied practice pack; a credited crypto balance alone does not meet their agreement.

Kojo sends a screenshot. It shows “Transfer submitted,” 30 DEMO tokens and a transaction identifier. “All done,” his message says. He asks her to hand the desk to his driver.

Nia nearly treats the tick as a receipt. Then she asks a more precise question: what does “submitted” establish?

The practice record on the correct fictional network says Pending. Harbour's own practice record shows no credit. The screenshot has not established receipt. Nia says she will wait for the stated conditions rather than guess from the sender's screen.

For this exercise, Harbour requires the specified asset and destination on the correct network, five confirmations and its own processing step. These are invented conditions, not a rule for every service. Nia checks that the asset, network, destination and amount match the supplied instructions.

Later, an updated network record shows a successful transfer with five confirmations. Harbour independently shows Credited: 30 DEMO. Nia can now recognise that the crypto balance has been credited under the exercise's conditions. The first screenshot alone could not establish that result.

There is a final distinction. She also requested a fictional conversion and payout. Its record says Payout pending. Her bank practice record has no corresponding incoming payment. Credited crypto has not proved that local money has arrived. She recognises the credited crypto balance, but keeps the desk until the independently checked local-money receiving record meets their stated agreement.

Nia's useful move was to ask which result the evidence supported at each stage. She did not assume every record was false, and she did not treat one established step as proof of the next. Depending on the agreement, unresolved evidence can mean waiting, requesting clarification or choosing another route.

For your own reading of a payment claim, ask: What is claimed? What record independently supports it? What still remains unconfirmed? This fictional case is a thinking exercise, not an instruction to accept crypto or release goods under a universal rule.

articles.title: Ethereum researchers explore checks on transaction outcomes
articles.body_html:
Ethereum researchers are exploring a way to check whether a transaction produces an intended result, alongside checking what a person agrees to sign.

In a 5 October 2026 research post, the Ethereum Foundation's Access Cluster described “native transaction assertions”: rules that would compare the state before and after an action and reject changes that break those rules. A rule might require a minimum amount received, limit spending, or preserve an account's control settings.

The problem is understandable without learning the engineering detail. Agreeing to a request does not necessarily guarantee the economic result you expected. A misleading interface can ask for different authority from what you intended; conditions can also change before an otherwise intended request executes. The researchers distinguish these problems and discuss where existing request explanations, simulations and contract checks have limits.

This is proposed protection, rather than a feature this article establishes as available in your wallet. The post discusses EIP-7906 as one possible approach and says it is being considered for inclusion, without confirmed inclusion in the named upgrade. The linked proposal and network status require their own checks before anyone treats that protection as deployed.

The rule itself also needs a trustworthy source. An interface that has been compromised could supply a rule that permits the unwanted result. A check is useful only when its conditions reflect independently established user intent or an appropriate standing policy. Its presence alone is not a guarantee.

There are practical limits too. The post describes protection within one transaction on one network, rather than a complete guarantee across a journey spanning networks or service providers. Under the described approach, an assertion failure would undo the transaction's action changes, while the included failed transaction could still consume a network fee.

For learners, the useful connection is to our permissions and transaction-status lessons: inspect the authority being requested, distinguish a prediction from confirmed execution, and ask which part of the journey a protection actually covers. A research announcement does not establish a safer asset, price outlook or reason to sign an unfamiliar request.

Source: Ethereum Foundation Access Cluster research post, 5 October 2026.

Read further: Permissions and combined practice and Ethereum introduction.

hubs.title: Bitcoin
hubs.body_html:
Bitcoin can refer to a network and to its native asset, commonly labelled BTC. The network records transfers according to its rules. A wallet helps a person interact with those records and authorise activity; the assets are not simply files sitting inside the wallet app.

Start by separating the asset, the network and any provider holding a balance for you. A service's BTC account, a self-custody arrangement and a token representing bitcoin through another system have different conditions. A familiar name does not make every receiving route interchangeable.

Bitcoin's price can move substantially. A transfer's network status does not establish a local payout, and the ability to receive bitcoin does not settle a country's legal or provider conditions. Learn the mechanics before deciding whether a particular use suits you.

Useful reading: basics in M-01; custody in M-03; transfer review in M-06; verification in M-07. Published relevant articles appear here as available. A quiet news period does not remove the value of the introduction.

hubs.title: Ethereum
hubs.body_html:
Ethereum is a network that supports transfers and smart-contract execution. Ether, commonly labelled ETH, is its native asset. Other tokens can operate through Ethereum without becoming the same asset as ETH.

Those distinctions matter when reviewing a request. A transfer, contract interaction and token-spending approval may give different authority or have different results. Know what the action authorises, which network it uses and which asset or representation is involved. A successful network record does not automatically establish provider credit or a later payout.

Related networks and services can use familiar address formats and labels. Receiving support must still be checked against exact current instructions. Fee estimates also depend on the action and network conditions; a low advertised fee is not a complete transfer review.

Start here: M-01 for network/asset basics, M-04 for routes, M-06 for fees and M-08 for authority. The wallets and scams topics connect the concepts to everyday decisions.

hubs.title: USDC
hubs.body_html:
USDC is a Circle-issued token that aims to track the US dollar. A target value, a market quote and the amount you can obtain through a particular conversion route are different things. Conditions matter at each step.

USDC has issuer-native deployments on multiple networks. A specific deployment and a third-party wrapped representation need separate identification. Matching tickers or address appearance do not establish that a receiving service accepts a transfer. Confirm the exact representation, selected network and current instructions together.

Direct issuer redemption also has eligibility conditions. The inspected Circle non-EEA terms refer to an eligible Circle Mint account; holding a token does not establish access to that route. Other services add their own account, conversion and withdrawal rules. An issuer's statement is not our independent reserve assurance or a local-availability guarantee.

Useful reading: Why stablecoins can surprise you, Same name, different route, Stablecoins, M-04 and M-05 when published.

hubs.title: Wallets and custody
hubs.body_html:
A wallet helps someone interact with a crypto system. It does not tell you by its name who controls transfers or how access can be recovered. A service account, self-custody wallet and shared-control arrangement can have different responsibilities.

Learn to ask who holds transaction authority, which actions need approval and what recovery route actually applies. A password reset may restore access to a service account. A compatible recovery phrase may restore keys in some self-custody designs. Neither is a universal process for every product.

Protect signing secrets and examine consequential requests. A receiving address is different from a private key or recovery phrase. This website never needs your real secrets or wallet connection for learning. Support instructions should be reached through an independently verified official channel.

Start with: Who controls a wallet?, custody/recovery in M-03 and permissions in M-08. Related news can add context without becoming a product recommendation.

hubs.title: Scams and trust
hubs.body_html:
A believable message can still ask you to take an unsafe or unverified action. Urgency, familiar branding, a friend forwarding a link or a payment screenshot cannot replace evidence about the request itself.

Practise identifying what is being claimed and what authority the requested action gives away. Requests for signing secrets deserve particular care. A signature or spending permission may have consequences beyond the label shown in a message. Verify through an independently reached official source rather than the sender's preferred link.

You do not have to prove someone committed fraud before declining an unverified request. Pause when evidence is missing and avoid sending more money or secrets to a stranger claiming they can repair a loss. If a real incident occurs, follow appropriate genuine reporting/support routes; this topic is education rather than individual recovery assistance.

Useful reading: M-02, M-08, What proves a payment? and phishing. Serious cases use direct English rather than jokes.

hubs.title: Stablecoins
hubs.body_html:
Stablecoins aim to track a reference value, often a currency. They use different mechanisms and can have different issuers, collateral, restrictions and redemption arrangements. The shared category name does not make them interchangeable.

Distinguish the target from the price offered in a market, direct issuer redemption from service conversion, and a credited token balance from a local-money payout. Each depends on its own conditions. A peg can be disrupted; a quoted rate and a small fee still need review as part of the whole route.

Receiving compatibility matters too. Identify the exact token representation, selected network and supported destination instructions. Do not treat a wrapped representation or a matching ticker as proof of acceptance.

Start with: Why a stablecoin can surprise you, USDC, M-05 and L-04.2 when published. USDC is one scoped teaching example, not a universal model or an endorsement. Relevant published coverage can follow this introduction without a promise of constant news.

glossary.title: Crypto asset
glossary.body_html: A digital asset whose ownership or use is recorded through a crypto system. The term includes assets with different designs and purposes; it does not mean every asset is money, a company share or legally classified the same way. Identify the particular asset and relevant rules before interpreting a claim about it. Related: Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins.

glossary.title: Blockchain network
glossary.body_html: A system of participants and rules that maintains a blockchain record and processes activity. Different networks have different assets, fees and supported actions. A familiar address format does not prove that two networks share receiving support. For a transfer, the selected network must match the destination's applicable instructions. Alias for discovery: network. Related: token representation, receiving address.

glossary.title: Wallet
glossary.body_html: Software or another interface used to interact with a crypto system and manage access or authorise activity. Assets are represented by system records rather than stored as ordinary coins inside the app. Wallet designs differ in who controls keys and how recovery works. Read the particular arrangement rather than assuming every wallet is self-custody. Related: custody, private key.

glossary.title: Custody
glossary.body_html: The arrangement for controlling access to assets and authorising their movement. A provider may hold keys, a person may control them directly, or authority may be shared. Custody affects responsibilities and recovery, but the label alone does not establish safety or availability. Ask who can act, what approvals are required and what restrictions apply. Related: wallet, recovery phrase.

glossary.title: Receiving address
glossary.body_html: An identifier used for a destination within a crypto system. Check the complete destination and selected network through current receiving instructions. Some services also require a memo or tag. A valid-looking address does not establish the intended recipient, supported asset or provider credit. An address may be shared for receiving where appropriate; signing secrets are different. Related: memo/tag, private key.

glossary.title: Private key
glossary.body_html: Secret cryptographic information used to create authorised signatures under a particular system's rules. Someone obtaining a usable key may gain dangerous transaction authority. It is different from a public receiving address and should not be pasted into a message or this learning website. Wallet arrangements can require more than one key or approval. Related: signature, custody.

glossary.title: Recovery phrase
glossary.body_html: A secret sequence of words that can restore related keys in compatible wallet designs. It is not a universal recovery method for every wallet or service account. Protect it according to the specific verified arrangement; anyone obtaining a usable phrase may gain control. This website never needs your actual phrase. Aliases: seed phrase; mnemonic phrase. Related: wallet, private key.

glossary.title: Signature
glossary.body_html: Cryptographic evidence created with a signing key for specified data or an action. What a signature authorises depends on the request and system; some requests have consequences beyond sign-in. Inspect the actual authority rather than relying on a friendly label. A signature does not independently prove someone's real-world identity or a promised later payment. Related: spending approval.

glossary.title: Transaction
glossary.body_html: A request or recorded action processed under a crypto network's rules. Its status may be pending, successful or failed, depending on the system and action. Being included in a record does not always mean the intended action succeeded. Check the relevant result, asset movement and conditions rather than treating every visible transaction as payment receipt. Related: transaction identifier, confirmation.

glossary.title: Transaction identifier
glossary.body_html: An identifier used to locate a transaction record on a particular network, often called a transaction hash. It is a starting point for verification, not proof of a successful payment by itself. Use the correct network and inspect the actual status, destination and relevant asset movement. A screenshot containing an identifier still needs independent checking. Related: explorer.

glossary.title: Gas
glossary.body_html: A measure of computational work used by Ethereum and some related systems to price execution. Gas units and the price paid for those units are different quantities. The action, network rules and current conditions affect the fee. Other networks can use different fee models. Do not treat an estimated fee as a guarantee of completion or receipt. Related: network fee.

glossary.title: Network fee
glossary.body_html: A charge associated with processing activity under a network's rules. It differs from provider, conversion or payout charges. The fee asset may be different from the asset being transferred. Some included failed executions can still incur a fee. Confirm the applicable model and quoted conditions rather than assuming rejection, failure and successful transfer have identical costs. Related: gas, spread.

glossary.title: Stablecoin
glossary.body_html: A crypto asset designed to track a reference value, such as a currency. Mechanisms and conditions differ. The target does not guarantee a market price, direct redemption eligibility or an amount received through local conversion. Identify the particular design, issuer or collateral and route before relying on a stability claim. Related: peg/reference value, issuer redemption.

glossary.title: Peg / reference value
glossary.body_html: The value a pegged asset aims to track. A token targeting USD 1 does not establish that every market or conversion quote equals USD 1. The mechanism may be stressed or fail to maintain the target. Keep the intended reference, actual offered price and final proceeds separate when evaluating a claim. Related: stablecoin, conversion.

glossary.title: Issuer redemption
glossary.body_html: Exchanging an eligible asset directly through its issuer under applicable terms. Holding a token does not automatically qualify someone for that route; account, jurisdiction and other conditions can apply. Selling through another service is a different arrangement. Check the particular issuer's current terms rather than generalising one token's redemption rules to all stablecoins. Related: conversion.

glossary.title: Conversion
glossary.body_html: Exchanging one asset or currency for another through a specified route. The quoted rate, spread, charges, availability and timing affect the result. A displayed crypto balance is different from completed conversion and from local-money payout. Use supplied fictional inputs for practice; this glossary supplies no live rate, available provider or permitted country route. Related: spread, issuer redemption.

glossary.title: Spread
glossary.body_html: The difference between quoted buying and selling prices, or another specifically stated price comparison. A route may incorporate costs through its quote rather than a separately labelled fee. Ask which prices are being compared and what the actual proceeds would be. A low visible service fee does not by itself make a conversion route cheaper. Related: conversion, network fee.

glossary.title: Token representation
glossary.body_html: The particular form in which an asset is represented within a system, such as an issuer-native token deployment or a third-party wrapped version. Similar names and prices do not establish equivalent rights or receiving support. Identify the exact representation and network, then check current destination instructions. Related: blockchain network, stablecoin, receiving address.

glossary.title: Memo / tag
glossary.body_html: An additional destination detail some receiving systems require to identify the intended account or purpose. It can be necessary alongside an address. Check whether the particular route requires it, and use the exact supplied detail. Do not assume every network or provider uses one, or that address-format validation proves the full receiving instructions are satisfied. Related: receiving address.

glossary.title: Confirmation
glossary.body_html: Evidence of a transaction's inclusion and subsequent network progression as defined by the particular system. How confirmations are described and counted varies. A provider may state its own crediting requirement and processing step. Meeting a confirmation count does not independently prove provider credit or a local payout. Related: finality, transaction, explorer.

glossary.title: Finality
glossary.body_html: The degree or condition under which a network treats an outcome as settled against reversal under its rules. Some systems use explicit finality conditions; others provide increasing confidence as the record progresses. Finality is network-specific and does not establish provider credit, conversion or bank/mobile-money receipt. Read the applicable model rather than applying one universal count. Related: confirmation.

glossary.title: Spending approval
glossary.body_html: Permission, in systems supporting it, for a specified address or contract to spend certain assets according to defined conditions. It is different from checking a balance or making one direct transfer. Inspect who receives authority, which asset and allowance are covered, and what revocation can change. A familiar logo or small initial request does not explain the full permission. Related: signature.

glossary.title: Explorer
glossary.body_html: A tool for viewing a network's records. Establish which network it shows and reach a trustworthy source independently. Inspect relevant status, destination and asset movement; search results and coloured ticks can require interpretation. An explorer record does not by itself verify a provider's account credit or a separate payout. This glossary does not select or endorse an explorer service. Related: transaction identifier.

glossary.title: Phishing
glossary.body_html: A deceptive request designed to obtain secrets, access or consequential actions by appearing trustworthy. It can arrive through messages, fake support, websites or other channels. Verify independently and inspect what is requested. Never give this website your signing secrets. Recognising missing evidence is enough to pause; you do not have to prove the sender's intent first. Related: signature, recovery phrase.
